intro: Out in Kaditz a lime that half burned down in 1818 still stands, held up from inside by roots that turned into stems; it is probably Dresden's oldest tree. Its rival is an oak in the Dresdner Heide, listed as a boundary marker in 1679. Upriver at Pillnitz, a camellia planted in 1801 survived a 1905 fire inside a shell of frozen hose water. In Blasewitz a copper beech made a clinic move 25 metres, and an oak of about 1650 lost its twin in 2025. Out west, five sweet chestnuts at Oberwartha have a lane named after them.
meta_description: Thirty-two notable Dresden trees: a lime in Kaditz that half burned in 1818, a camellia that survived a 1905 fire in ice, and five 400-year-old chestnuts.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Dresden is the Kaditzer Linde, a large-leaved lime in the churchyard of the Emmauskirche in Kaditz, and the city itself declines to say how old. Its sign calls the tree many centuries old and then adds a thousand years with a question mark, because a fire in 1818 destroyed the side of the trunk facing the parsonage and no ring count has been possible since. What stands there now is a half shell over nine metres round, held up on the inside by former roots that turned into supporting stems. Estimates in the literature run from 500 to 1000 years. Its nearest rival on this page is the Rieseneiche in the Sauerbusch, a pedunculate oak in the Dresdner Heide that a forest record of 1679 already listed as a boundary marker, estimated at up to 700 years. Next comes the lime on the Laubegast riverbank, planted or sown around 1680. Just over the city line in Freital, the sources put the Grenzeiche anywhere between 1570 and 1770, and the Plague Oak of Pesterwitz went in in 1681. If you know of a dated study that narrows the lime's age, tell us.
question_meta: The Kaditzer Linde, a lime in the Kaditz churchyard, is Dresden's oldest: estimates run from 500 to 1000 years and the city's own sign asks the question.
question_context: Dresden keeps an official register of natural monuments, Naturdenkmale, published as a public Wikipedia table and cross-checked for five trees here against Stadtwiki Dresden. At least twenty-one of the thirty-two trees on this page carry that designation; the Babisnau poplar holds it from its own district, and the Plague Oak of Pesterwitz and the Grenzeiche from the town of Freital. The Splittereiche is protected as part of the listed Grosser Garten; the Luthereiche in the Dresdner Heide and the Moreau Oaks are Saxon Kulturdenkmale, and the Luther Oak of Kleinluga is both. The Saengereiche, the Bismarckeiche and the Pillnitz camellia have no official designation. The Albertplatz plane, the Fetscherplatz oak, the Räcknitz horse chestnut and the Heide pine were all protected on 3 January 1985; the Trinitatisplatz oak waited until February 2024. The Kaditzer Linde, probably the oldest, carries a range, because its trunk has been too damaged for too long to be counted. Several other ages come from a recorded planting date, which beats a growth-rate guess but is not a ring count; the Schulmeisterlinde has its planter's own entry of 1622 in the church chronicle. The Brauteich oak and the Konigsbrucker Strasse elm have no age recorded.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Dresden?
faq.a: The Kaditzer Linde, a large-leaved lime in the churchyard of the Emmauskirche in Kaditz. Estimates run from 500 to 1000 years and the city's own sign puts a question mark after the higher figure, because a fire in 1818 destroyed half the trunk and left nothing to count.

faq.q: Can I see all thirty-two trees in one walk?
faq.a: No. The Zerr-Eiche and the Fetscherplatz oak both stand in Johannstadt, a short tram ride apart, and Albertplatz, the Konigsbrucker Strasse elm and the oak at the Barnsdorfer Strasse fork sit north of the river in the Neustadt. The Grosser Garten, the Laubegast lime on the Elbe and Kaditz, 6 km northwest of the old town, are each a trip of their own, and the Rieseneiche is a forest walk in the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide. In Blasewitz the copper beech of Naumannstrasse and the Hüblerstrasse oak stand about 450 metres apart, while the Pillnitz camellia, the five chestnuts at Oberwartha, the weeping beech in the Helfenberg manor park on the eastern slopes and the Babisnau poplar on its plateau south of the city are each a trip of their own. In Kaditz the Schulmeisterlinde stands 15 metres from the Kaditzer Linde, and the Meschwitz Oak in St. Pauli Cemetery is about 150 metres from the Barnsdorfer Strasse oak. The Moreau Oaks stand on the Räcknitzhöhe south of the old town, with the Volkspark Räcknitz horse chestnut nearby, the Albert Oak of Wasaplatz is in Strehlen, the Bühlau oak is on the north-eastern edge, and the village-square oaks of Kleinluga, Oberpoyritz and Kauscha are outings to Dresden's south and south-east. The Brauteich oak at Langebrück and the pine in the eastern Dresdner Heide are forest outings, and the Plague Oak of Pesterwitz and the Grenzeiche stand about a kilometre apart in Freital, just west of the city.

Nearly all of them. Thirty stand on open public squares, village squares and streets, in public parks and a manor park crossed by a walking route, in a churchyard and a cemetery, on a monument meadow, beside a lane, a road, a stream or a riverside cycle path, on open fields or in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide, with no ticket needed. The Pillnitz camellia stands in the paid grounds of Schloss & Park Pillnitz, and its glass house opens only in the flowering season. The copper beech of Naumannstrasse stands in a medical centre's garden and can be seen from the street.

faq.q: Why are several of these trees protected under the same 1985 date?
faq.a: Dresden's city council designated the Albertplatz plane and the Fetscherplatz oak as natural monuments in a single resolution on 3 January 1985. The fingered-leaf horse chestnut in Volkspark Räcknitz and the pine in the Dresdner Heide were protected on the same date. The Trinitatisplatz oak had to wait far longer, gaining the same protection only in February 2024.

trees.name: The Zerr-Eiche of Trinitatisplatz

location.address: Trinitatisplatz, opposite the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche, Johannstadt, Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing on a public square (Trinitatisplatz) opposite the church
trees.transport: Tram stop Trinitatisplatz, right on the square (news coverage of a nearby tram diversion names conflicting line numbers across sources, so no specific line is stated here)
trees.story:
Dresden got round to protecting this oak in February 2024, some 130 years after the city planted it. It was raised at the municipal nursery on the Tatzberg and set out on Trinitatisplatz in 1895, facing the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche. Fifty years later the air raids of February 1945 came over Johannstadt, and the oak came through them without serious damage. It then came through the winters that followed, when firewood was scarce enough in Dresden that standing trees disappeared into stoves, and this one was left alone.

It is a Turkey oak, a southern European species with deeply cut leaves and acorns sitting in shaggy, mossy cups rather than the smooth ones a German oak wears. The case for designating it called it the strongest of its kind in Dresden and the third strongest in Saxony, on grounds of age, rarity, form and genetic value.

The trunk measures about 3.84 metres round, worked from a recorded stem diameter of 122 centimetres, although the city's own register line says more than four metres. Nobody has reconciled the two figures and neither is worth much fuss.

Twenty metres tall, standing in the open on a public square with a tram stop at its foot, it is about as easy to reach as a protected tree gets.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak facing the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche across Trinitatisplatz, with a tram stop at its foot.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Albertplatz

location.address: Albertplatz, on the traffic island toward Bautzner Strasse, Innere Neustadt, Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing on a traffic island in the middle of a public square, accessible at any time
trees.transport: Albertplatz tram and bus interchange, right on the square
trees.story:
This plane tree lives on a traffic island. Albertplatz is one of the busiest interchanges in Dresden, a circle of tram and bus routes in the Neustadt, and the tree stands out in the middle of it toward Bautzner Strasse, twenty-five metres tall with a crown roughly as wide as it is high.

It was planted around 1885, when that ground was open and quiet. Everything else arrived later: the trams, the traffic, the night of 13 February 1945 and the long rebuilding after it, forty years of the GDR, and the Neustadt's more recent turn into the loudest quarter in the city. The tree has stayed put through all of it on its own island, which is the closest thing to a fixed point Albertplatz has. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, by the same council resolution that protected the oak on Fetscherplatz.

A London plane is a hybrid of the American and the Oriental plane, and it was planted across European cities for exactly the qualities on show here. It takes heat, compacted soil and dirty air better than almost anything else with a trunk, and it sheds its bark in pale plates through the summer instead of letting the grime build up.

Its trunk measures 3.30 metres round. Both the register and the city's own record agree on the figure, which is rarer than it sounds.

trees.how_to_recognise: The plane tree standing alone on the traffic island toward Bautzner Strasse, in the middle of the Albertplatz interchange.

trees.name: The Oak of Fetscherplatz

location.address: Fetscherplatz, Johannstadt, Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing on a public square, visible and reachable at all times
trees.transport: Tram stop Fetscherplatz, directly beside the tree
trees.story:
In 1949 an architect built a tram shelter around this tree rather than move either of them. Herbert Schneider put his waiting kiosk on Fetscherplatz so close to the trunk that the roof had to curve to make room for the oak, four years after the air raids, in a city with more urgent things to be careful about. The two have shared the corner ever since.

The tree is an overcup oak, a North American species and an unlikely thing to find holding down a square in Johannstadt. It went in around 1900, when the place was still called Fuerstenplatz, and it has since put out a crown about thirty-two metres across, wider than the tree is tall. That crown is effectively the roof of the square. Twenty-five metres up, 3.35 metres round at the trunk, and the only real shade anyone waiting for a tram is going to get.

Dresden protected it as a natural monument on 3 January 1985, in the same council resolution that covered the plane tree on Albertplatz.

If you are there in autumn, look at the acorns on the ground. The cup on this species swallows almost the entire nut, which is where the name comes from and the quickest way to tell it apart from every other oak in the city.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak whose crown roofs Fetscherplatz, with a curved 1949 tram shelter built up against its trunk.

trees.name: The Splittereiche

location.address: Grosser Garten, on the open lawn roughly 40 metres south of the Mosaikbrunnen (Mosaic Fountain), Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing in the open on a public lawn inside the Grosser Garten park, open during park hours
trees.transport: Enter the Grosser Garten and walk to the Mosaikbrunnen; nearest tram stops are around Strassburger Platz or Lenneplatz, roughly a 10-15 minute walk into the park (approximate, not independently timed)
trees.story:
This oak is named after its wounds. On the nights of 13 and 14 February 1945 the bombing of Dresden reached the Grosser Garten, and splinters tore open one side of the trunk along roughly eight metres of its height. The tree survived. The damage is still there and still obvious, which is how it came to be called the Splittereiche, the splinter oak.

It was already old when that happened. An assessment made in the 2010s put it at between 250 and 300 years, a range nobody has narrowed since and which is itself a decade out of date by now. It stands twenty-seven metres tall with a trunk over six metres round, out on open lawn a short walk south of the Mosaikbrunnen, so you see the whole shape of it from a distance before you get to the scar.

On 8 May 2017, the seventy-second anniversary of the end of the war in Europe, a memorial plaque went up beside it carrying a line from Mark Twain: time may heal all wounds, but it is a lousy cosmetician. The year after, the city fitted metal sheeting over the damaged flank, because visitors picking at the old injury were making it worse.

We have not found it listed individually in Dresden's register of natural monuments. It stands inside a protected historic park instead, and it is the tree people in that park come to find.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak on the open lawn south of the Mosaikbrunnen, with a visible bomb-splinter scar running up one side and a 2017 memorial plaque beside it.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Kaditzer Linde
trees.age_estimate: somewhere between 500 and 1000 years; the city's own sign asks the question rather than answering it

location.address: Emmauskirchhof, Altkaditz 27, 01139 Dresden

trees.story:
Half of this tree burned in 1818 and what holds the other half up is its own roots.

A fire that year took eighteen farms, thirty barns and the parsonage of Kaditz, and the lime beside the church went with them. The side facing the parsonage died outright. What survived is a half shell of trunk, and the city's sign on it explains the trick that kept the thing alive: the stems standing inside the hollow are former roots that turned into supports.

Dresden calls it the oldest tree in the city and will not put a number on it. The sign says many centuries old, then adds a thousand years with a question mark after it. Nothing can be counted, because the trunk has been damaged too often for rings to survive. A parish account of 1909 put the circumference at twelve and a half metres. A measurement at chest height in 2007 gave 9.6. Both figures are in the record and nobody has reconciled them.

Since 1829 its heaviest limbs have been held up, first on timber, now on steel anchors and cables. The smaller of its two stems stopped leafing out in 2021 and died. The larger one did not.

A bench runs in a ring around the base.
trees.access: Free. In the churchyard of the Emmauskirche, open in daylight. A wooden bench rings the trunk.
trees.transport: Tram 9 to its terminus at Kaditz, Riegelplatz, then about ten minutes on foot into Altkaditz. About 6 km northwest of the old town.

trees.how_to_recognise: Not a trunk but a standing half shell, wide open on one side, with a curved wooden bench built around its foot and steel cables running up into the crown. A war memorial with a stone eagle stands a few metres away.

trees.name: The Rieseneiche of the Sauerbusch

location.address: Sauerbusch, Dresdner Heide (forest district Hofewiese), near Langebruck

trees.access: Free. Public forest (Sachsenforst, Dresdner Heide); a signposted educational trail 'Rieseneichen' (run by the Heimatverein Weixdorf) leads to it. Forest paths, no ticket.
trees.transport: Not verified. Remote forest stand in the far north-east of the Heide near Langebruck, well over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot or by bike from Langebruck or Weixdorf. Check current timetables before quoting a stop.
trees.story:
In 1679 a forest protocol listed two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers. One of them is still alive. Its main stem broke off at about fifteen metres long ago, so what stands now is a trunk about 6.60 metres round carrying a crown made of single limbs. The local account puts it at up to 700 years, which is an estimate rather than a count; somewhere between four and seven centuries is the honest reading.

The two oaks were probably mast trees, kept for their acorns, and both were placed under protection in 1938, although some sources give 1958. In 1993 a fire started by children killed the second one. This one carried on.

It has not carried on easily. The forest district describes it as being in the last stage of its life, although it is still vital. Heavy growth covers the stem, one side is almost stripped of bark, and parts of it are held together with concrete. Even its height is disputed: the Wikipedia article says about 22 metres, the city's natural monument list says 14.

A signposted trail, the Rieseneichen path kept by the heritage society in Weixdorf, leads through the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide to the trunk. It is a forest walk from Langebruck or Weixdorf rather than a city stroll, and this oak is the reason to make it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the snapped-off main stem on a trunk about 6.60 metres round, one side almost bare of bark and patched with concrete. It stands on the signposted Rieseneichen trail in the Sauerbusch.

trees.name: The Oak of Barnsdorfer Strasse

location.address: Junction of Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse, Leipziger Vorstadt

trees.access: Free. A freestanding tree at a street junction on public ground.
trees.transport: Not verified in detail; inner-city district north-west of the Neustadt, on the B170 side near Hansastrasse. Check the nearest tram stop before quoting.
trees.story:
This oak probably started out in a beer garden. It was planted around 1880 on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork, and the pub on that tip, Zur Gruenen Aue, stood until 1960. The written record says the tree was probably part of the pub's garden, and nobody has managed to get further than probably. The pub is gone. The oak, about 140 years old, has outlasted it by more than sixty years.

It has grown to about 25 metres with a crown some 30 metres wide, and its trunk measures 4.45 metres round. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, the same day the city protected the Kaditzer Linde, an oak on Doebelner Strasse and a pine in the Heide.

About 150 metres to the north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand two more oaks of the same generation, the Marschall oak and the Meschwitz oak, planted around 1870 or 1880 and treated by the city as memorial trees. We have not checked how freely the cemetery can be walked, so this page sends you only to the junction.

The newest photographs of this oak date from 2015, and we have no recent confirmation that it is still in good health. If you pass the fork and it is standing, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the freestanding oak, 4.45 metres round, on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork. It stands about 100 metres south-east of where Hechtstrasse leaves Hansastrasse.

trees.name: The Linden on the Laubegast Riverbank

location.address: Laubegaster Ufer, by house no. 17, Altlaubegast

trees.access: Free. Stands on the outside of the ice-protection wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17, beside the road; just north of the driveway the road is closed to cars and is a foot and cycle path forming part of the left-bank Elbe cycle route.
trees.transport: Not verified; Laubegast is an eastern Elbe-bank district. Check the nearest tram stop and walking time before quoting.
trees.story:
In March 1940 the biggest Elbe flood of the twentieth century drove ice floes 40 centimetres thick against this lime for ten to fifteen hours. The floes hit both the tree and the masonry surround its owner had built in 1913. The ice tore a wound about half a metre tall around half the trunk, and the ridge it left still shows at roughly 1.5 metres up.

The lime was already old by then. The local account has it planted or sown in the second half of the seventeenth century, most likely in the 1670s or around 1680, and in 1997 the owner wrote of a 320-year-old linden. That puts it somewhere near 340 today. The house behind it at number 17 is a youngster by comparison, built in 1879 for a Saxon court marshal and now a listed monument in its own right.

It is a small-leaved lime, about 20 metres tall with a trunk 3.90 metres round, standing outside the ice-protection wall beside the road. The paving over its roots was replaced with cobbles to protect them, and the city made it a natural monument in June 1999.

Just north of the driveway the road closes to cars and becomes part of the Elbe cycle route, and two more protected trees stand about 500 metres away in each direction along it: black poplars at number 1 and a black pine at number 39.

trees.name: The Fluttering Elm of Konigsbrucker Strasse

location.address: Konigsbrucker Strasse 49, on the pavement side between houses 49 and 51, Aussere Neustadt

trees.access: Free. The elm stands on the pavement side of the property in front of the houses at Konigsbrucker Strasse 49 to 51 and is visible and reachable from the public pavement on a main street; the pin marks the tree on the street frontage.
trees.transport: Not verified in detail; Aussere Neustadt on the Konigsbrucker Strasse tram corridor, close to the centre. Check the nearest stop before quoting.
trees.story:
Dresden protected this elm in 2015 for surviving something most of its kind have not. Dutch elm disease, spread by fungi that arrived from Asia, has killed elms across Europe, and when the city went looking in the early 2010s for its most valuable trees, 39 of them at 29 sites, it picked this European white elm as an exceptional specimen that was still healthy.

It is not a park tree. It stands on Konigsbrucker Strasse in the Aussere Neustadt, on the pavement side in front of numbers 49 and 51, and it sets the look of the street: about 30 metres tall, with a crown some 20 metres across and a trunk 3.57 metres round. Trams run past it along the Konigsbrucker Strasse corridor.

It was not the city's first protected elm. A white elm in Altubigau and the elms on Sachsenplatz had been natural monuments since 1999, so this one joined a short list rather than starting it.

Two things we do not know. Nobody has documented when it was planted, so this page gives no age; if you know, tell us. And the newest photographs on record are from 2019, so if you walk past and it is still standing over the pavement, that is worth a message too.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall elm, about 30 metres, on the pavement side of Konigsbrucker Strasse in front of numbers 49 and 51. Its trunk measures 3.57 metres round.

location.address: Dresdner Heide, forest section 109 (Revier Langebruck), about 150 m north-west of the crossing of Radeberger Strasse and Schneise 8

trees.access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst), a short way off the Schneise 8 forest ride; no entry charge.
trees.transport: Not verified. Inside the Heide, over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot from the Radeberger Strasse side. Check timetables before quoting a stop.

trees.story:
In October 2002 a hurricane found a fork in this beech that nobody knew was failing, and more than a third of the crown came down. Two years earlier Dresden had made it a natural monument, measured at about 35 metres tall, 5.70 metres round and with a crown some 28 metres across. At that point only one beech in the city was bigger, the one behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude.

What stands in forest section 109 of the Dresdner Heide today is the tree that came out of that storm: lower than the 35 metres in the record and lopsided where the crown went. Every photograph on file was taken after the damage, so they show the beech as a visitor will meet it rather than as it looked on the day it was designated.

The age given in 2000 was about 250 years, and that was an estimate then. Add the years since and it lands somewhere around 275, give or take a few decades. The ordinance protects a ring of 18 metres around the trunk along with the tree itself.

trees.story:
This oak was planted for a song festival, and the sources still argue over whether it is the oak they planted. In July 1865 Dresden hosted the first German Sängerbundesfest, and a festival hall went up on this stretch of the Elbe meadows. On 13 November that year, according to the Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv, Heinrich Hartwig and two gardeners planted a memorial oak where the hall had stood.

That is where the agreement ends. A festival booklet from 1925 says the November tree was the singers' own gift, a young oak that choirs from around Leipzig had carried through the procession in a tub, and that it later had to be replaced after vandals got to it. Rainer Pfannkuchen, once head of Dresden's nature-protection authority, reads it the other way: the festival oak died of drought, and the November 1865 planting was already the replacement. So the trunk in front of you is either the 1865 tree, which would make it about 160 years old, or a later stand-in, and nobody has settled which.

Whichever it is, the open ground has suited it. In 1994 it stood 26 metres tall under a crown 20 metres wide, and its girth grew from 3.80 to 4.26 metres between 1994 and 2018. Since 2013 it has had a neighbour it never asked for: the Waldschlösschenbrücke now crosses the river about 25 metres away, and the Elbe cycle path runs past its feet.

trees.story:
This oak was planted to honour four hundred years of the Reformation, and it has spent a century failing to look the part. On Sunday 28 October 1917, with Germany deep in the First World War, it went into the ground in the Dresdner Heide to mark the anniversary of Luther's 95 Theses. A memorial stone carrying a Luther inscription was set beside it, and the two together are now a protected Saxon cultural monument, number 09217019.

The ground was against it from the start. This corner of the forest is dry sand over Lusatian granite, and the oak never thrived: local coverage in 2017 called it a puny specimen, which is fair. Nobody comes here for the size of the trunk. What makes it worth the detour is the setting, beside a forest ride in the Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park section of the forest, and the small act of remembrance that keeps being renewed around it. For the Luther year of 2017 the benches were replaced and a table added, and one of the benches now carries a quotation from Luther himself.

It makes a good stop on a walk through the Heide rather than a destination of its own. Two things nobody has recorded: which species of oak it is, and how big it has managed to grow. If you know either, tell us.

trees.story:
The stone beside this oak has changed its mind about who it honours. The tree was planted in 1895 for Otto von Bismarck's 80th birthday, and the sandstone block next to it was dedicated to him too, with his portrait in a bronze medallion. The medallion went missing shortly after the Second World War. In 1998 the block was given a new bronze plaque, this time remembering Hofgärtner H. S. Neumann, 1829 to 1880, the court gardener who designed the Waldpark itself.

So the oak has outlasted the man it was planted for and the monument that explained it. At about 130 years old it is no giant, and nobody has published its girth or height. What it offers is the park its stone now commemorates, and a small lesson in how a memorial gets rewritten when the century moves on.

Be warned before you go: there is no information sign, and the Bismarck Oak stands as part of a group of trees. Our pin is approximate, close to the spot but not on the trunk, so you will have to pick the right oak yourself. The stone is the giveaway. Find the sandstone block with the Neumann plaque on the Lothringer Weg, west of the tennis courts, and the oak is the one beside it.

trees.story:
In January 1905 this camellia's winter house burned down at about minus 20 degrees, and the water from the fire hoses froze around the plant in a shell of ice. It survived, and sprouted again that spring.

It has stood on this spot since 1801, when the court gardener Carl Adolph Terscheck planted it. The camellia reached the Dresden court somewhere between 1770 and 1790, so 225 years at Pillnitz are documented; the palace's owners, the Saxon state palaces administration, put it at over 250. A favourite story says it is one of four plants the botanist Carl Peter Thunberg brought back from Japan in the 1770s. Kew has no record of that, and the claim is increasingly doubted. A 2015 study at TU Dresden found it almost genetically identical to the old camellias of Caserta, Campobello in Portugal and Greifswald, which points to cuttings from one shared stock.

Strictly it is a shrub grown into a tree: almost nine metres high, with a crown nearly eleven metres across. In 2025 it became the first camellia in Germany to be named a Historic Camellia by the International Camellia Society.

From October to May it lives inside a heated 13-metre glass house that weighs 54 tonnes and runs on rails. In summer the house rolls aside and the tree stands in the open park. The owners call it the largest and oldest of its kind north of the Alps. Come in March, when up to 35,000 crimson flowers are open.

trees.story:
Legend says that when this poplar blooms, a war is about to end. People reported it in 1870, in 1918 and in 1943, when Victor Klemperer noted it in his diary on 23 May. What appears is not really a bloom but the fluffy white seed of the ripe fruit, and it does not come every year.

The landowner Johann Gottlieb Becke planted the black poplar in 1808 to mark the edge of his property. By 1884 it drew so many visitors that a farmer wanted it felled to keep them off his land, and the local mountain club bought the tree for 300 marks to save it. A viewing frame went up beside it the following year and has been rebuilt in 1922, 1963 and 1999. In the war of 1866 it served as a lookout, and surveyors used it as a sighting mark.

The weather has been harder on it than people were. A thunderstorm on 20 July 1967 took a third of the crown, storms in 1996 took most of the rest, and the main stems were later topped. The 2025 survey gives 15 metres of height where 2004 recorded 26, a trunk 5.50 metres round, and only a few side branches still in leaf. A clone grown from its cuttings was planted a few metres away in 2006, in case.

It stands alone on an open plateau outside the city, and the platform looks over the Elbe valley to Saxon Switzerland and the Ore Mountains.

trees.story:
In the early 1970s a new clinic in Blasewitz was moved 25 metres to spare this tree. The polyclinic had been drawn on the axis of Villa Marienlust, which meant the copper beech in its garden would have had to come down. Volunteer conservationists negotiated, the building went up further south-east with an angled wing to join it to the villa, and the change cost 30,000 marks, judged at the time a great but necessary sacrifice.

The beech was planted in 1849, already four years old, in the villa's 17,000 square metre grounds. The villa now houses a medical centre, the Ärztehaus Blasewitz, whose own history page counts more than 177 years. It has grown about 25 metres tall, with a crown about 24 metres across, so broad and low that it is said to grow like a giant shrub. The register gives its girth as 5.35 metres, but that was measured 30 centimetres above the ground, where any trunk is wider than at the usual chest height.

The city made it natural monument number 34 in January 1985, and a plaque on the tree says so. It stands in the medical centre's garden. The crown can be seen from Naumannstrasse, and we have not confirmed whether the garden is open to walk into; if you have been in, tell us. The surviving oak of Hüblerstrasse stands about 450 metres to the south-west.

trees.verify_notes: THIS IS ONE TREE NOW, not the pair. Natural monument ND 35 listed 'Stieleichen Hueblerstrasse' (Baumgruppe, 2 oaks), pair protected since 22 Aug 1938 and by council ruling 3 Jan 1985. One of the two was felled on 22 June 2025 because of fungi, viruses and bacteria and lost stability (dawo-dresden.de, de.wikipedia; the city's press release pm_067 exists, but the page returned HTTP 503 so was not read; the headline '375 Jahre alte Eiche verliert Kampf gegen Pilz' came through search only). dawo-dresden.de: 'Nur wenige Meter von der gefaellten Eiche steht noch ihr gesunder Baumbruder, der ebenfalls um 1650 gepflanzt wurde' (healthy). The city plans a replacement of a more climate-adapted oak species in autumn 2025 or spring 2026 (so a young tree may now stand beside it; the writer should not confuse them). The writer must make clear that the page is about the surviving one, and that the felled one was its twin. Figures (de.wikipedia, before the felling, for the pair): height about 23 m, crown diameter about 22 m, girths 4.65 m and 4.80 m: I could not establish which girth belongs to the survivor, so girth_cm 480 is the larger of the two and is approximate; do not state a girth for the survivor with precision. Age: a resistograph measurement in 1995 suggests the trees stood by 1650 (wikipedia); the press and dawo say 'planted around 1650' and '375 years'. That is a derived, not a documented, figure, so 350-400 is the honest band. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, Commons photos of Hueblerstrasse 23/25 dated 2025-09-03 (after the felling) and a Commons photo of the felled stump 2025-07-13. Pin: the register coordinate 51.050885,13.802852 and 10+ Commons files geotagged within 12 m; two oaks stood a few metres apart on the verge, one remains, so the pin is on the spot to within metres; the visitor will see the remaining oak and the stump or new planting. Story material: until 1998 the oaks stood with half their trunks in the roadway; protection discs were built in 1998 and the soil to 60 cm depth replaced with a suction vehicle, which uncovered an old granite-paved road half a metre down beside the oaks; root bridges at neighbouring driveways, crown care. The oaks predate the villa district: around 1866 the surroundings were still unbuilt and the road was the old route Striesen-Blasewitz-Loschwitz; the crown form suggests they once stood free and served for acorn mast. The house at Hueblerstrasse 23 was destroyed in WW2 while the oaks survived, between listed villas 21a and 25. trees.story:
Until June 2025 there were two of them. These pedunculate oaks stood a few metres apart on the verge of Hüblerstrasse for something like 375 years, until fungi, viruses and bacteria left one unstable and it was felled on 22 June. This is the survivor, which the local press called its healthy brother. The stump of the twin stands beside it, and the city planned to plant a young oak of a more climate-tolerant kind in its place.

The age comes from a resistograph test in 1995 that suggested the pair already stood by 1650, so read it as somewhere between 350 and 400 years rather than a birth certificate. Either way they are older than the villa quarter around them. Around 1866 this was still open ground and the road was the old route from Striesen through Blasewitz to Loschwitz; the shape of the crowns suggests the oaks once stood free, perhaps kept for their acorns to fatten pigs. The house at number 23 was destroyed in the Second World War. The oaks came through.

Until 1998 they stood with half their trunks in the roadway. That year protective barriers went in, root bridges were laid at the neighbouring driveways, and the soil was replaced to 60 centimetres with a suction vehicle, which uncovered an old granite road half a metre down. Before the felling they were about 23 metres tall, with trunks of 4.65 and 4.80 metres; nobody recorded which girth belongs to the survivor.

trees.name: The Five Brothers of Oberwartha

location.address: Fuenf-Brueder-Weg at the entrance to the Taennichtgrund, 01156 Oberwartha, Dresden

trees.access: Free. Beside a public lane and footpath, the Fünf-Brüder-Weg, at the edge of the village on the way into the Tännichtgrund valley. A signposted natural monument, open-air, no entry needed.
trees.transport: In the far west of Dresden, about 13 km from the Altstadt. The nearest rail stop is Niederwartha, on the line from Dresden Hbf towards Elsterwerda-Biehla; we have not timed the walk from there.

location_site.name: Fuenf-Brueder-Weg at the edge of the Taennichtgrund

trees.verify_notes: Ensemble of five sweet chestnuts, one obvious place to stand, one natural monument (ND 67 per Stadtwiki Dresden; protected since 1958 per a search result, not read at source). de.wikipedia (a designated natural monument; the register itself was not read) gives: heights 12 to 25 m, crowns 10 to 20 m, girths at 1.30 m between 4.15 m and 6.20 m; planting 'in the first half of the 17th century' (de.wikipedia, Stadtwiki and the Dresden-Elbland tourism board all agree; one web page says 1624, which none of the others confirm, so do not use it). girth_cm 620 is the thickest of the five, not an average. Age is the sources' 'first half of the 17th century', i.e. roughly 375 to 425 years; band widened for safety. Alive: lifecheck RECENT (iNaturalist observation 2026-04-08 at the spot) and the tourism board still lists it. Pin: three sources give three points within about 25 m of each other (Wikidata 51.080838,13.598625; Dresden-Elbland 51.080877,13.598992; Commons geotag 51.080837,13.598671); the five trunks are spread along the path, so the pin is the group, location_precision approximate with a 40 m site. Tell-apart line for the writer: they stand along the Fuenf-Brueder-Weg where it leaves the village; the thickest is 6.20 m round. Legends (all three reported by de.wikipedia, none documented): a girl abducted by a dragon whose five brothers died looking for her and who planted the trees in their memory; six monks from Kloster Altzella planted six chestnuts before a crusade, only five grew and only five monks came home; five brothers who went out into the world and returned rich, each planting a tree. Stadtwiki: they replaced five lindens that were sacred to the Nisan people at the Gertrud spring (a spring shrine); this is a Stadtwiki claim only, treat as folklore. The lane and the stream (Fuenf-Brueder-Bach) are named after the group. Photos: Commons category Naturdenkmal Fuenf Brueder Oberwartha Dresden (several files, lead file listed on the Wikidata item 'Naturdenkmal Fuenf Brueder Oberwartha Dresden 04.JPG'); not judged. It is a day trip west of the centre, not a walk from the other Dresden trees; the Oberwartha lime (Naturdenkmal Dorflinde Oberwartha, Q68667250, 51.0777,13.6024, 'heritage monument') is about 450 m away (by coordinates; not researched) as a possible pair.

best_time.label: October, when the chestnuts drop along the lane

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the five old chestnut trunks lining the Fünf-Brüder-Weg where it leaves the village for the Tännichtgrund, beside the natural monument sign. The thickest is 6.20 metres round.
trees.story:
Nobody agrees why there are five. One legend has a girl carried off by a dragon and her five brothers dying in the search for her, with the trees planted in their memory. Another has six monks from Altzella monastery planting six chestnuts before a crusade: five grew, and five monks came home. A third has five brothers who went out into the world, came back rich and planted a tree each. Dresden's city wiki adds that they replaced five limes at a spring once sacred to the Slavic Nisani, which is folklore too.

What the sources do agree on is the date, the first half of the 17th century, which makes these sweet chestnuts roughly 400 years old. They stand along a lane at the edge of Oberwartha, on the far western rim of Dresden, where it runs down into the Tännichtgrund valley. The lane is the Fünf-Brüder-Weg and the stream below is the Fünf-Brüder-Bach, both named after the trees, which tells you how long they have been the landmark here.

They run from 12 to 25 metres tall, with crowns 10 to 20 metres across, and their trunks measure between 4.15 and 6.20 metres round at chest height. The group is a protected natural monument, signposted beside the lane. Come in October, when the chestnuts drop.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Helfenberg Park

location.address: Park of Schloss Helfenberg, south of the manor house, Am Helfenberger Park, Dresden-Helfenberg

trees.access: Free. The park south of the manor house is crossed by the Elbhangwanderweg, a public walking route.
trees.transport: About 9 km east of the Altstadt. Bus 98B (Borsberg to Niederpoyritz via Schönfeld) is the only public transport in Helfenberg; we have not timed the walk from its stop.

photo.attribution: Dr. Bernd Gross, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.story:
Of the two weeping beeches this park was protected for, one now lies on the grass. Storm Niklas pulled the larger and more imposing of the pair out of the ground on 31 March 2015. Dresden left the fallen tree where it fell, as habitat for wildlife, and planted a young one into its root zone.

The survivor is the one to walk to, and it has had the harder life. In 1985 a hole in its trunk, a metre and a half up, was filled with concrete, and it has since lost a large limb. The pair were described as about 20 metres tall with crowns some 25 metres across, the biggest and gnarliest weeping beeches in the area. Measurements disagree: the city's green-space office lists 3.90 and 4.35 metres round, while baumkunde.de taped this one at 4.70 metres in 2018.

Look low on the trunk for the bulge where it was grafted onto an ordinary beech, which proves a gardener made it rather than nature. Some say 300 years. More likely it went in when James Ogilvy, 7th Earl of Findlater, had the park remodelled in the English style between 1806 and 1811; a city publication of 2008 put the beeches at about 180 years. Either way it has outlived the earl, the secretary who inherited his estate, and its own twin. The district council protected both trees on 23 January 1958.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the concrete filling a hole in the trunk at about 1.5 metres, and by the fallen trunk of its twin, uprooted in 2015, left lying in the grass. It stands in the park south of the Helfenberg manor house.

best_time.label: late October, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper

trees.name: The Schulmeisterlinde of Kaditz

location.address: Altkaditz 27, Emmauskirche churchyard, between the south choir tower and the churchyard wall

trees.access: Free; in the churchyard of the Emmauskirche, listed as publicly accessible by baumkunde.de. Plaque beside the tree.
trees.transport: Tram 9 to its terminus at Kaditz, Riegelplatz, then about ten minutes on foot into Altkaditz; it stands 15 metres from the Kaditzer Linde. About 6 km northwest of the old town.
trees.story:
Few trees come with their planter's own words. On 8 April 1622 Paul Schulze, schoolmaster of Kaditz, wrote in the church chronicle that he had planted a lime beside the churchyard wall, facing the school, and added a line of hope: God help that it may grow well. It did. Four centuries later the Schulmeisterlinde is the oldest tree in Dresden whose planting date and reason are both on record. Schulze put it in at Easter, when the new school year began, four years into the Thirty Years' War, opposite the village school that stood across the street.

It has not had an easy four hundred years. In the 1920s the road was widened and the churchyard wall was rebuilt hard against its trunk. On 8 August 1970 the fire brigade cut the crown back drastically because the hollow trunk threatened to break, and it was pruned again in 1999. The hot, dry summers of the late 2010s hit it too. What stands now is a barrel of a trunk 4.4 metres round, hollow all the way through, under a crown reduced to about 8 metres.

It has a famous neighbour. Fifteen metres to the south-west stands the Kaditzer Linde, older, wider and far better known, and most visitors come for that one. The schoolmaster's tree is the one with a birth certificate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow, barrel-shaped trunk, 4.4 metres round, pressed against the churchyard wall with a plaque beside it. It stands by the south choir tower, 15 metres north-east of the half-shell Kaditzer Linde.

trees.name: The Meschwitz Oak of St. Pauli Cemetery

location.address: St.-Pauli-Friedhof, Hechtstrasse 78, section B, near the mortuary chapel

trees.access: Free; the cemetery is open to visitors (baumkunde.de: publicly accessible). A plaque stands at the tree. Normal cemetery courtesy applies.
trees.transport: St. Pauli Cemetery in the Leipziger Vorstadt, north of the Neustadt; the tree is about 125 m east of the main gate on Radeburger Strasse. We have not checked the nearest tram stop.
trees.story:
Germany's largest known shingle oak began as a father's grief, and for fifty years nobody remembered whose. In autumn 1880 Friedrich Wilhelm Meschwitz, Dresden's forest master and the man who opened the Dresdner Heide to walkers, buried his son Wilhelm here. Wilhelm was 19, the only one of three sons who could have followed his father into the forest. Meschwitz brought a young North American oak from the forest botanical garden at Tharandt and planted it beside the family grave. In 1888 he was laid there himself.

In 1960 the grave was cleared. The oak stayed, and its story left with the headstone. It was simply a big tree in section B of St. Pauli Cemetery until 2010, when Rudolf Schroeder of the Saxon Heimatschutz association rediscovered it and the city entered it in its tree register as probably the finest shingle oak in Saxony. The German Dendrological Society has listed it as a record tree since 2012. A plaque went up on 18 October 2013, on Juergen Lambrecht's initiative, and with it came the name: the Meschwitz Oak.

In 2020 it measured 3.8 metres round and 28.5 metres tall, and the 2012 plaque figures gave its crown 33 metres across. Cables and safety pruning now keep that crown safe above the people walking beneath it. Our pin is approximate, because two published coordinates disagree by about 100 metres; the plaque is the surer guide.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque at its foot naming it the Meschwitz-Eiche, and by its height, about 28 metres. It stands in section B, about 125 metres east of the main gate on Radeburger Strasse, 50 metres east of the mortuary.

trees.name: The Moreau Oaks

location.address: Moreau-Denkmal, Moreauweg / Raecknitzhoehe, on the meadow 'Franzosenhoehe'

trees.access: Free, open meadow with the monument; the whole meadow ('Franzosenhoehe') and monument are a listed Kulturdenkmal. Slope, no ticket, no gate described in the sources.
trees.transport: On the Räcknitzhöhe south of the Altstadt, across the street from Räcknitz Park. We have not checked the nearest bus or tram stop.
trees.story:
Beneath these three oaks lie a general's legs. On 27 August 1813, in the Battle of Dresden, the French general Jean-Victor Moreau was fighting on the allied side, next to Tsar Alexander, when a cannonball shattered both his legs. He died six days later. A monument went up on the spot in 1814, commissioned by the Russian governor-general Repnin-Wolkonski, and on 4 November that year the amputated legs were buried beneath it in an urn. That same November three pedunculate oaks were planted around the stone, one for each ally: Russia, Prussia and Austria.

They did not start well. In 1836 the writer Ferdinand Stolle reported that the oaks looked sickly and had given no shade even in 1830, on ground judged poor for them. They stand today regardless, carrying the scars: broken branches, pruned crowns, and a cavity in one trunk that has been surgically closed. Their crowns have grown together into one, and their stems now press against the monument's stone border.

Nor did they grow evenly. One trunk is 4.75 metres round, the other two 3.00 and 2.55. The meadow, called the Franzosenhöhe, is protected together with the monument as a heritage site, which is why the oaks carry no natural-monument status of their own. The inscription still reads: Moreau, the hero, fell here at Alexander's side.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as three oaks with crowns grown together, ringed close around a stone monument whose inscription names Moreau; the thickest trunk is 4.75 metres round. They stand on the Franzosenhöhe meadow off Moreauweg.

trees.name: The Luther Oak of Kleinluga

location.address: Teichplatz (village square), between Teichplatz 8 and 9, Kleinluga

trees.access: Free; on the open village square (Teichplatz) with a pond nearby, public ground. Memorial stone and protection plaques at the tree. Farmsteads border the square, the tree itself is on the square plot (Flurstueck 2).
trees.transport: Kleinluga, in the south-east of Dresden, about 10 km from the Altstadt. We have not checked the bus connection; use the VVO journey planner.
trees.story:
Schoolchildren planted this oak on 10 November 1883, Martin Luther's 400th birthday, and it has run the village square ever since. The pupils came from the school at Grossluga, whose district took in the little village of Kleinluga, and they set it in the middle of the Teichplatz, near the pond. A memorial stone went in front of it.

The young oak was planted in the German Empire and has stood through every state that followed. It is now about 20 metres tall, with a crown about 22 metres across and a trunk 4.10 metres round, by the city's own nature-protection records. Nothing else on the square comes close: the farmsteads keep to its edges and the oak takes the middle.

In 1998 and 1999 the square was redesigned around it and the memorial stone was renewed. On 10 June 1999 the city council made the tree natural monument ND 88, with a protected zone reaching three metres beyond the edge of its crown and never less than 15 metres from the trunk. Together with its stone it is also a listed heritage monument, so the Luther Oak is protected twice: once as nature, once as history.

It stands about 10 km south-east of Dresden's old town. Another village-square oak, at Oberpoyritz about 5 km to the north-east, was protected by the same council on the same day.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only big oak in the middle of the Teichplatz, with a granite memorial stone at its foot and natural-monument plaques. It stands between Teichplatz 8 and 9, near the pond.

trees.name: The Village Square Oak of Oberpoyritz

location.address: Dorfplatz, Oberpoyritz, east of the north-south village street

trees.access: Free; stands on the open village square (Dorfplatz), public ground, with protection plaques on the trunk.
trees.transport: Oberpoyritz, in Dresden's outer south-east, about 10 km from the Altstadt. We have not checked the bus connection; use the VVO journey planner.
trees.story:
This oak was slowly dying of the village around it, and Dresden dug up its square to save it. Through the 1980s and 1990s its crown thinned and paled. The blame fell on the paving laid around the trunk, and possibly on a leaking gas main in the root zone. In 1998 the city rebuilt the site: the gas pipe was re-routed, and the roots were bridged under the driveways and the pavement. The diggers found thick roots five metres beyond the edge of the crown, which says something about how far an oak reaches for what it needs. Within a few years the crown had recovered.

It stands free on the Dorfplatz of Oberpoyritz, the village's landmark. The city's records give it about 25 metres of height, a crown about 25 metres across and a trunk 4.30 metres round. The Viehbotsche brook runs between the tree and the house plots to the east and joins the Graupaer Bach about 40 metres to the south.

On 10 June 1999 the city council made it natural monument ND 85, on the same day as the Luther Oak of Kleinluga, with a protected zone of at least 16 metres around the trunk. Its age is an estimate: in 2008 the city's environment office put it at about 150 years, which would place it in the middle of the 19th century. Nobody recorded the planting. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single free-standing oak on the Dorfplatz, 4.30 metres round, with natural-monument plaques on the trunk. It stands east of the village street, with the Viehbotsche brook running past on its east side.

trees.name: The Albert Oak of Kauscha

location.address: Village square on the street 'Zur Eiche', Kauscha

trees.access: Free; on the open village square of Kauscha, public ground. Granite memorial stone and protection plaque at the tree.
trees.transport: Kauscha, in Dresden's south, roughly 8 km from the Altstadt. We have not checked the bus connection; use the VVO journey planner.
trees.story:
In 1945 a laundry owner named Menzel plastered over the gold lettering on the stone in front of this oak, to hide a king's name from the approaching Soviet army. The king was Albert of Saxony. The oak had gone in as a young tree in spring 1898, on the village square of Kauscha, for his 70th birthday and his 25th year on the throne. Several Albert oaks were planted around Dresden for that double jubilee, at Waldschlösschen, Loschwitz, Stetzsch, Strehlen and Weissig. This is the largest known of them.

It is also the one that outgrew its age. Its trunk measured 5.10 metres round in 2008, under a crown about 35 metres across and 25 metres high. In 2004 the Sächsische Zeitung called it Dresden's mightiest tree. Yet it has no old-age bark, the city's official gazette noted the same year, unlike the 17th-century oaks of the Hüblerstrasse and the Sauerbusch: a big tree, not an old one.

In the 1950s children scraped the plaster off the stone. By 1999 little of the lettering was legible, and the stone has since been reconstructed. The oak had its own trouble: after the 1990s switch to natural gas, a leaking pipe through its root zone drove the oxygen out of the soil and thinned the crown. The pipe was replaced in 1998, and once Kauscha joined Dresden in 1999 the city rebuilt the site and the tree recovered markedly. The street through the village core is now called Zur Eiche.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the granite memorial stone at its foot and the trunk, 5.10 metres round, under a crown about 35 metres across. It stands alone on the village square, on the street called Zur Eiche.

trees.name: The Albert Oak of Wasaplatz

location.address: Wasaplatz, Strehlen, Dresden

trees.access: Free. Stands on the public Wasaplatz square in the middle of a busy junction; a footpath runs right up to the trunk. Street traffic on the other side.
trees.transport: A tram line runs through Wasaplatz (per de.wikipedia, since 1928); stop name and timetable not verified, check before quoting.
trees.story:
This oak was planted as a birthday present for a king, and has spent most of its life negotiating with traffic. It went into the ground on Wasaplatz in Strehlen in April 1898, on the 23rd or the 24th depending on which record you trust, for King Albert of Saxony's 70th birthday and his 25th year on the throne. Several Albert oaks went in around Dresden for that double jubilee. This one got a fenced decorative plot ringed with birches.

The square did not stay quiet. A tram line has run through Wasaplatz since 1928, a main road now presses hard against one side of the tree, and its crown is pruned back regularly so that traffic clears it. In 1991 a cable was laid through its root zone and the roots were cut. It kept growing anyway. The most recent measurements put it at about 21 metres tall, with a crown some 24 metres across and a trunk 3.85 metres round; the city's older designation figures give 20 metres and 3.65.

Dresden made it a natural monument in 1999. At under 130 years it is not an ancient tree and does not pretend to be. It is a royal anniversary that kept its leaves, holding the middle of a busy junction while the city works around it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single large oak in the middle of the star-shaped Wasaplatz, its trunk 3.85 metres round, with tram tracks curving past. A main road runs hard against one side of it.

trees.name: The Oak of the Bühlau Village Green

location.address: Quohrener Strasse, former village green (Dorfanger), Bühlau, Dresden

trees.access: Free. Stands on the former village green beside Quohrener Strasse, public ground, no ticket.
trees.transport: Not verified. Bühlau is a north-eastern district; the Dresden tram line to Bühlau ends nearby but the stop name and walking time were not checked.
trees.story:
This oak is wider than it is tall: when it was measured in 1999 its crown spread about 28 metres across, on a tree about 25 metres high. It stands on what was once the village green of Bühlau, beside Quohrener Strasse, and a few metres to its south-east a small stream, the Quohrener Abzugsgraben, rises out of the ground.

It is not a veteran. The city's 2008 brochure on its natural monuments put it at about 140 years, which places its planting somewhere around the 1860s or 1870s. That is an estimate, not a record, and nobody has written down who planted it or why.

Dresden protected it in 1999, and the ordinance gives three reasons: its particular form and character, what it does for the look of the place, and dendrological grounds. At designation the trunk was 1.26 metres thick at a metre off the ground, about 3.95 metres round; the city's own list gives 4.00.

Two things we would like help with. The pin is approximate: two published coordinates for this tree sit about 60 metres apart, and ours is the one beside the spring. And the most recent dated photographs of it we know of were taken in May 2015. If you have stood under it since, tell us it is still there, and where exactly.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, about 28 metres across and wider than the tree is tall. It stands on the old village green beside Quohrener Strasse, a few metres north-west of where the Quohren stream rises.

trees.name: The Fingered Horse Chestnut of Volkspark Räcknitz

location.address: Volkspark Räcknitz, north-west corner, just north of the entrance from Stadtgutstrasse, Dresden

trees.access: Free. Public park (Volkspark Räcknitz), the tree stands at the edge of the raised lawn by the Stadtgutstrasse entrance.
trees.transport: Not verified. Räcknitz lies in the south-west of Dresden; check the tram or bus stop near Stadtgutstrasse before quoting a walk time.
trees.story:
This horse chestnut belongs to a variety that normally grows as a shrub, and it is about 20 metres tall. 'Digitata', the fingered-leaf form, has been spreading out of France since 1864. This specimen was grafted onto an ordinary horse chestnut, and above the graft it has gone on to raise a trunk of its own, under a crown about 18 metres wide.

It came out of the Reichsgartenschau of 1936, the national garden show Dresden hosted that year, as one of the rare trees the exhibitors left to the city when the show was over. No planting year was written down, so its age of about 90 is counted from the show rather than from a record of the day it went in.

In January 1985 Dresden's council made it a natural monument, and it was the only tree from the then district of Dresden-Süd in that resolution. The city's documentation gives its trunk as 3.05 metres round at 0.7 metres up; the German Dendrological Society's list of record trees has it at 3.53 metres at breast height in 2010.

It stands in the north-west corner of Volkspark Räcknitz, at the edge of the raised lawn just inside the entrance from Stadtgutstrasse. A garden show lasts a summer. Its shrub that turned into a tree is still here, ninety years on.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fingered leaves, the rare 'Digitata' form, and the multi-stemmed crown above a grafted trunk. It stands at the edge of the raised lawn just north of the Stadtgutstrasse entrance.

trees.name: The Oak of the Brauteich

location.address: Brauteich, west of the built-up area of Langebrück, north of the railway line, Dresden

trees.access: Free. Stands on open land beside the Brauteich pond; the city's 2008 hiking and cycling route past five Naturdenkmale in the Dresden north includes it. Exact path and any fence not checked.
trees.transport: Not verified. Langebrück has a railway station; the oak lies west of the village on the north side of the line. Check the walk time before quoting.
trees.story:
This oak is protected less for its size than for the way it looks beside a pond. It stands on open land west of Langebrück, beside the Brauteich, a pond fed by a stream called the Braugraben, and it is the picture the two make together that the city's documentation singles out: the tree's form, and its interplay with the water.

It has been on the books since 1958, when the district council of Dresden registered two natural monuments at Langebrück, this oak and a spring pond, the Quellteich. The figures are respectable rather than record-breaking. The city gives a height of about 22 metres, a crown about 20 metres across and a trunk 4.70 metres round, less massive than the Albert oak at Kauscha. And the form that earned it protection has had a hard time since: rot and a lightning strike have broken out part of the crown.

Nobody has recorded its age, and the history of the tree is described as largely unknown. If you know when it was planted, or own an old photograph that shows it, tell us.

In 2008 the city put it on a walking and cycling route past five natural monuments in Dresden's north, together with the giant oak in the Sauerbusch; they are kilometres apart, so it is a ride rather than a stroll. The pin is approximate, and the last dated photographs we know of are from 2017 and 2018. If you go, tell us how it is doing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad crown, part of it broken out by rot and lightning, beside the Brauteich pond. It stands on open land west of Langebrück, north of the railway line.

trees.name: The Plague Oak of Pesterwitz

location.address: An der Winzerei, Oberpesterwitz (Pesterwitz), Freital, near the St.-Jakobus-Kirche

trees.access: Free. Stands beside the public road An der Winzerei at the entrance to the village on a bend; a protection sign stands in front. No bench or verge to linger on (per the Dresden Elbland tourism page), so view from the roadside.
trees.transport: Not verified. Pesterwitz belongs to Freital, about 10 km south-west of central Dresden; bus or tram link and travel time were not checked, so confirm that it is within 30 minutes before presenting it as a Dresden day trip.
trees.story:
This oak was planted in 1681 as a timber investment, and nobody ever collected. The parish of Pesterwitz put it in together with several other trees, meaning to sell the wood one day. The others are gone. This one still stands on the bend at the entrance to the village, on the road called An der Winzerei near the church of St. Jakobus.

Its name comes from the calendar rather than from any record of why it went in: 1680 and 1681 were plague years, and the tree became the Pesteiche, the plague oak.

It has come close to the axe since. In the Second World War it was marked to be felled for a tank barrier, and it survived that too. Today it is over 20 metres tall, the regional tourism office says almost 22, with a trunk more than five metres round. The crown needs help to hold together: it is secured with ropes, and another brace went in with the pruning of 2023.

The custom of naming a tree for an epidemic did not end with it. In 2021 a young oak was planted near the old Winzerei and called the Corona oak.

Pesterwitz belongs to the town of Freital, just west of Dresden, which protects the oak as one of its natural monuments. It stands right on the road with no verge or bench, so this is a tree to look up at from the roadside rather than to sit under.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ropes and brace holding its crown together and the protection sign in front of it. It stands right on the road An der Winzerei, on the bend at the entrance to the village.

trees.name: The Grenzeiche of the Green Valley

location.address: Gruenes Taelchen on the Hammerbach, where the path from Kohlsdorfer Strasse to Kohlsdorf crosses the stream, Freital (Pesterwitz/Potschappel boundary)
location.neighbourhood: Oberpesterwitz / Potschappel (Freital), just west of Dresden

trees.access: Free. Stands on the bank of the Hammerbach in the Gruenes Taelchen, a flaechennaturdenkmal, beside a public connecting path; baumkunde.de's register records access as publicly accessible (checked 2022).
trees.transport: Not verified. Freital-Potschappel, about 8 to 10 km south-west of central Dresden; stop and walk time not checked, confirm before presenting it as a Dresden day trip.
trees.story:
The sources disagree about when this oak was planted by two full centuries: somewhere between 1570 and 1770. What they agree on is where. It stands in the Grünes Tälchen, the little green valley of the Hammerbach, on the old boundary between Pesterwitz and Potschappel, and it may have been planted to mark that line. That is how it got its name, the Grenzeiche, the boundary oak.

Whatever its age, it has the build of an old tree. When it was measured in February 2022 its trunk was 6.20 metres round, it stood about 29 metres tall and its crown spread more than 22 metres. The trunk is hollow. Somebody once tried to set fire to it, and it survived; on that same 2022 visit it was recorded as vital, with no fungi.

So the age here is a band rather than a number, roughly 250 to 450 years depending on which local history you follow, and one tree register settles on the low end. If a dated document for the planting exists, we would like to see it.

The oak is one of the natural monuments of the town of Freital, just west of Dresden, and the Plague Oak of Pesterwitz, planted in 1681, stands about a kilometre away. Here the setting is quieter: the bank of a stream, where the public path from Kohlsdorfer Strasse to Kohlsdorf crosses the water.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk, 6.20 metres round. It stands alone on the bank of the Hammerbach, where the path from Kohlsdorfer Strasse to Kohlsdorf crosses the stream.

trees.name: The Pine of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Eastern Dresdner Heide, about 60 m east of the Weissiger Weg between the Ochsensteig and the Bischofsweg, forest district Ullersdorf (compartment 43)

trees.access: Free. Public forest (Sachsenforst, Dresdner Heide), reached on foot from forest tracks; the trunk carries a Naturdenkmal plaque. About 60 m off the Weissiger Weg, no path to the trunk itself was verified.
trees.transport: Not verified. Remote forest stand in the north-east of the city, well over 30 minutes from the centre by public transport; reached on foot or by bike. Check current timetables before quoting a stop.
trees.story:
This pine has watched the forest around it be felled and grown back twice. Foresters count in rotations, the 80 to 140 years between planting a stand and cutting it, and this tree, which the city's documentation estimates at about 250 years old, has outlasted two of them. It was left standing each time, and now rises to about 25 metres over the open high forest of the Dresdner Heide.

It is not a giant. Its trunk is 2.75 metres round and its crown about 12 metres across. What makes it rare is age in a working forest, where pines are grown to be harvested; the estimate puts its start somewhere in the middle or later part of the 18th century.

In the 1970s volunteer naturalists proposed naming it the Karl-Jahn-Kiefer, after the forester who ran the Dresdner Heide forestry office from 1958 to 1975 and pushed for the landscape protection area of 1969. The name never caught on, though a sign bearing it has been photographed on the tree. Dresden made it a natural monument in January 1985, and its protection zone covers the whole crown and at least 18 metres around the trunk.

It stands about 60 metres east of the Weissiger Weg, between the Ochsensteig and the Bischofsweg, with a plaque on its trunk. The most recent dated photographs we know of are from June 2017. If you walk out to it, tell us it is still there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the natural monument plaque on its trunk and by how it towers over the open forest around it. It stands about 60 metres east of the Weissiger Weg, between the Ochsensteig and the Bischofsweg.
